summary:
At the Moon's south pole, the Sun stays right near the horizon, so even small crater rims can cast long shadows or block line-of-sight communication with Earth. When launch dates get delayed or mission plans change, teams have to re-check lighting and communication conditions across different candidate sites—a process that usually requires manual work across complex tools like JPL Horizons and Lunar Quickmap.

We built Lunar South Pole Mission Navigator to make this comparison fast and visual. Our tool combines an analytical MATLAB engine (using NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data and LRO LOLA elevation maps) with a standalone interactive web dashboard. Users can choose from a built-in list of candidate landing sites like Shackleton Rim and Mons Mouton, or enter any custom coordinates. With an interactive timeline slider and side-by-side comparison mode, anyone can track the Sun and Earth against the local terrain horizon, check countdowns to the next sunrise or Earthset, and compare total sunlight, longest darkness stretches, solar power potential, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows.
Note: We used Claude AI to assist with code generation and building the web interface alongside our MATLAB calculations.
details: What does it do & how does it work? Lunar South Pole Mission Navigator is an interactive mission-planning dashboard and analysis tool that evaluates solar illumination, energy potential, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows at the Moon's south pole. Users can select from a built-in list of key landing sites (such as Shackleton Rim, Mons Mouton, Malapert Massif, Nobile Rim, and Haworth Rim) or enter any custom coordinates. Using an interactive timeline slider, anyone can track the hour-by-hour movement of the Sun and Earth relative to the local mountain horizon, view live countdowns to the next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, or Earthset, and compare two sites or launch dates side by side. What benefits does it have? At the lunar south pole, the Sun stays very close to the horizon, meaning local crater rims can easily block sunlight or cut off direct communication with Earth. Normally, checking how a launch delay or site change affects visibility requires pulling raw tabular data from complex interfaces like JPL Horizons and manually cross-referencing elevation maps in Lunar Quickmap. Our tool turns that slow, technical workflow into an instant visual comparison. What is the intended impact of the project? For mission planners and engineers, it speeds up early landing site trade-offs and schedule-shift evaluations. For educators, students, and the general public, it makes the unique geometry of the lunar south pole—like continuous horizon-skimming sunlight and Earth libration—easy to see and understand without needing aerospace software expertise. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use? - Languages & Libraries: MATLAB for the core astronomical and terrain mask calculations, and HTML5, JavaScript, and Plotly.js for the standalone, zero-install web application. - Data & Software: NASA JPL Horizons API (for topocentric Sun and Earth ephemeris), LRO LOLA Digital Elevation Models (GeoTIFF DEMs) via Lunar Quickmap, GitHub Pages for hosting, and Claude AI to help write and structure parts of the code and web interface. How is our project creative? Instead of showing static tables or single-point charts, we combined a dual-scenario side-by-side comparison layout with an interactive timeline scrubber. Being able to drag a single slider and watch both the Sun and Earth move across two different crater horizons simultaneously—while seeing real-time countdown timers and energy metrics update—bridges the gap between a serious engineering calculator and an intuitive educational simulator. What factors did our team consider? - Lunar Geometry & Curvature: Spherical lunar curvature (R = 1737.4 km) when ray-tracing local 360-degree terrain masks from LOLA elevation data. - Angular Semi-Diameters: Finite angular radii of the Sun (0.265 deg) and Earth (0.95 deg), since partial limb visibility still provides power or signal. - Energy & Mission Constraints: Total sunlit percentage, longest continuous darkness stretch (critical for battery survival), solar panel power potential (Power Proxy based on solar elevation angle), and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication availability.
